hints: Think about what a base does with its lone pair on nitrogen when it meets $\text{H}^+$ in water.
Compare how many ethyl groups are attached to nitrogen in diethylamine versus ethylamine and what alkyl groups do to electron density.
Look at ethanamide, $\text{CH}_3\text{CONH}_2$, and ask where the nitrogen lone pair can go when a $\text{C=O}$ is next to it.
Order the three from most available lone pair to least available lone pair to give most basic to least basic.
walkthrough:
Picture basicity as lone pair donation**
Think of a base as a lone pair looking for a proton. For all three compounds the basic site is nitrogen. The easier that lone pair can form a new $\text{N-H}$ bond with $\text{H}^+$, the stronger the base. So you are really comparing lone pair availability.

Compare the two amines**
Ethylamine is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ and diethylamine is $(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2)_2\text{NH}$. Alkyl groups push electron density toward nitrogen by the positive inductive effect. With two ethyl groups, diethylamine has more electron density on N than ethylamine with one ethyl group, so its lone pair is more ready to accept $\text{H}^+$. That puts diethylamine as most basic of the three.

See why the amide is very weak**
Ethanamide is $\text{CH}_3\text{CONH}_2$. Do not treat it like an amine. The lone pair on N overlaps with the pi system of the adjacent $\text{C=O}$. You can draw it as delocalisation: $\text{N}$ lone pair moves to form $\text{C=N}^+$ and $\text{C=O}$ becomes $\text{C-O}^-$. Because the lone pair is partly tied up in this conjugation, it is very poorly available to pick up $\text{H}^+$. That makes ethanamide least basic by a large margin.

Final answer: diethylamine > ethylamine > ethanamide (most basic to least basic).
Basicity depends on availability of the lone pair on N to accept $\text{H}^+$.
Ethyl groups are electron donating, increasing electron density on N and making the lone pair more available, so secondary amine > primary amine.
In ethanamide the N lone pair is delocalised into the $\text{C=O}$ group, making it much less available.

hints: Recall what happens to pH of pure water versus a buffer when you add one drop of acid.
Remember the definition must include the condition of small amount of added acid or alkali.
walkthrough:
Fix the core idea of a buffer**
Imagine adding a drop of $\text{HCl}$ to water, the pH crashes. Adding the same drop to a buffer barely changes the pH. A buffer soaks up added $\text{H}^+$ or $\text{OH}^-$ using a large reservoir of weak acid and conjugate base.

Give the complete definition**
State both parts together: resistance to pH change, and the trigger is addition of a small amount of acid or alkali. Both ideas are needed for full credit.
Final answer: A solution that resists change in pH when a small amount of acid or alkali is added.

hints: Think of alanine $\text{H}_2\text{NCH(CH}_3\text{)COOH}$ as having a basic $\text{-NH}_2$ end that can mop up added $\text{H}^+$.
Think of the same molecule as having an acidic $\text{-COOH}$ end that can mop up added $\text{OH}^-$ to give water and $\text{-COO}^-$.
walkthrough:
Use the amine end to remove added acid**
When $\text{H}^+$ is added, the $\text{-NH}_2$ group acts as a base. It accepts the proton to become $\text{-NH}_3^+$. Write: $\text{H}_2\text{NCH(CH}_3\text{)COOH} + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{N}^+\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)COOH}$. The $\text{-COOH}$ stays unchanged here.

Use the acid end to remove added alkali**
When $\text{OH}^-$ is added, the $\text{-COOH}$ group acts as an acid. It donates a proton to $\text{OH}^-$ to make water, leaving $\text{-COO}^-$. Write: $\text{H}_2\text{NCH(CH}_3\text{)COOH} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{NCH(CH}_3\text{)COO}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. The $\text{-NH}_2$ stays unchanged here.

Final answer: $\text{H}_2\text{NCH(CH}_3\text{)COOH} + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{N}^+\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)COOH}$
$\text{H}_2\text{NCH(CH}_3\text{)COOH} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{NCH(CH}_3\text{)COO}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$

hints: Count the carbon chain in Fig. 7.1: two $\text{COOH}$ carbons plus three chain carbons, and remember skeletal lines hide C and H but show heteroatoms explicitly.
walkthrough:
Translate to lines and heteroatoms**
Glutamic acid is $\text{HOOC-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH(NH}_2\text{)-COOH}$. In skeletal form each $\text{CH}_2$ bend is a vertex with H atoms hidden. Draw a zigzag of three chain carbons between the two $\text{-COOH}$ groups. Show both $\text{C(=O)OH}$ groups fully and show $\text{-NH}_2$ attached to the carbon next to the lower $\text{COOH}$ (the alpha carbon). No $\text{C-H}$ labels are shown.

Final answer: Skeletal formula of $\text{HOOCCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)COOH}$: a 5 carbon chain shown as zigzag with $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{OH}$ at both ends and $\text{NH}_2$ on the alpha carbon.

hints: Recall ala-glu means the $\text{COOH}$ of alanine joins the $\text{NH}_2$ of glutamic acid with loss of water.
Remember the peptide link $\text{-CO-NH-}$ itself must be displayed, while alkyl side chains can be shown as $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$.
walkthrough:
Join COOH of ala to NH2 of glu**
Line up alanine on the left: $\text{CH}_3\text{-CH(NH}_2\text{)-COOH}$ and glutamic acid on the right: $\text{H}_2\text{N-CH(COOH)-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$. Remove $\text{OH}$ from the left $\text{COOH}$ and $\text{H}$ from the right $\text{NH}_2$ to eliminate $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Display the new link clearly**
Draw the product with a displayed amide: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)-C(=O)-NH-CH(COOH)-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$. Show the $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{N-H}$ of the peptide bond explicitly. Keep the free $\text{NH}_2$ on alanine and both $\text{COOH}$ groups of glutamic acid intact, one as part of the backbone and one in the side chain.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)CO-NH-CH(CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH)COOH}$ with the $\text{-C(=O)-N(H)-}$ peptide bond displayed.

hints: Compare buffer pH 6.0 with each isoelectric point to decide if each species is neutral, positive or negative.
Recall negative ions move toward the positive electrode and neutral zwitterions stay at the origin.
For the two negative species, think about which has smaller $M_r$ and so moves faster and further in the same time.
walkthrough:
Work out the charge from pH versus pI**
The isoelectric point is the pH where the amino acid has zero net charge. If buffer pH is above pI, $\text{COOH}$ groups are deprotonated and the species is negative. If buffer pH equals pI, net charge is zero. Here buffer pH is 6.0. Alanine pI is 6.0, so net zero. Glutamic acid pI is 3.2, so pH 6.0 is well above pI, so it is negative. The dipeptide ala-glu still contains the extra acidic side chain $\text{COOH}$, so it is also negative at pH 6.0.

Predict direction of movement**
In electrophoresis, positive moves to negative electrode and negative moves to positive electrode. So alanine stays where applied (marked X in the centre). Both glu and ala-glu migrate to the left toward the + electrode.

Separate by size**
Both migrants have similar charge but different mass. Glutamic acid is a single amino acid with lower $M_r$ than the dipeptide ala-glu. Smaller ions experience less friction and migrate faster. So glu travels furthest toward +, ala-glu stops between the origin and glu. Label all three spots clearly.

Final answer: Alanine stays at the origin (mixture applied here); glu and ala-glu move toward + electrode, with glu further toward + than ala-glu.
At pH 6.0 alanine is at its isoelectric point so exists as neutral zwitterion; glu (pI 3.2) and ala-glu are negatively charged at pH > pI.
Glu has lower $M_r$ than ala-glu so moves further.

hints: Use Fig. 7.3 and Table 7.1 to match each $\delta$ to a proton environment in $\text{G}$, $\text{H}_2\text{NCH(CH}_3\text{)COOCH}_3$.
Apply the $n+1$ rule: a proton with $n$ equivalent protons on adjacent carbons splits into $n+1$ peaks.
Remember integration gives number of protons responsible, and $\text{NH}_2$ protons exchange in $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ so are not seen.
walkthrough:
Assign the doublet at 1.4 ppm**
G is the methyl ester $\text{H}_2\text{N-CH(CH}_3\text{)-C(=O)-O-CH}_3$. The alkane $\text{CH}_3$ attached to $\text{CH}$ appears around $\delta$ 1.4. It sees one proton on the neighbouring $\text{CH}$, so $n+1 = 2$, a doublet. Integration is 3 H.

Assign the singlet at 3.5 ppm**
The $\text{O-CH}_3$ protons are next to electronegative oxygen, deshielded to $\delta$ 3.2 to 4.0. There are no protons on the adjacent carbonyl carbon, so $n = 0$, giving a singlet. Integration is 3 H and it is tall and sharp.

Assign the quartet at 4.0 ppm**
The $\text{CH}$ proton attached to both $\text{NH}_2$ and $\text{C=O}$ is deshielded to $\delta$ 4.0. It sees three equivalent protons on the neighbouring $\text{CH}_3$, so $n+1 = 4$, a quartet. Integration is 1 H. Note the $\text{NH}_2$ protons do not appear because they exchange with $\text{D}_2\text{O}$.

Final answer: $\delta$ 1.4: doublet, 3 H responsible, 1 proton on adjacent carbon; $\text{CH}_3$ next to $\text{CH}$.
$\delta$ 3.5: singlet, 3 H responsible, 0 protons on adjacent carbons; $\text{OCH}_3$ with no adjacent protons.
$\delta$ 4.0: quartet, 1 H responsible, 3 protons on adjacent carbons; $\text{CH}$ next to $\text{CH}_3$.

hints: Ask which protons in $\text{G}$ are attached to N and what happens to $\text{N-H}$ in $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ versus $\text{CDCl}_3$.
walkthrough:
Spot the labile protons**
The $\text{-NH}_2$ protons are labile. In $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ they rapidly exchange: $\text{R-NH}_2 + \text{D}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{R-ND}_2 + \text{HOD}$, and deuterium is invisible in proton NMR, so the peak vanishes. In $\text{CDCl}_3$ no such exchange occurs, so you see one additional signal for the $\text{NH}_2$ protons (around $\delta$ 1.0 to 5.0).
Final answer: One extra peak for the $\text{NH}_2$ group is seen in $\text{CDCl}_3$; in $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ the $\text{N-H}$ protons exchange for D and disappear.
